summary: The most probable root cause is CPU throttling of aa-sync starting around 09:55, which pushed its latency from about 90 ms to about 550 ms. portfolio-consumer calls aa-sync synchronously, so it began timing out from about 09:57. The portfolio-updates queue's consume_rate fell from about 49 to about 15 while publishing stayed near 40, and the backlog grew from 137 messages at 10:02 to 1573 by 10:59, which delays notifications. Request rate did not rise, so the throttling is likely from a reduced or mis-set CPU quota, or from a CPU consumer unrelated to request volume. This is unconfirmed because no quota or config data was retrieved. A separate, earlier receipt-delay signal in msg-delivery (from 09:02) is probably an independent issue that cannot be tied to portfolio-update notifications. Rate units and consumer rps do not reconcile with the observed backlog growth, so the exact mechanism has gaps.

hypotheses.statement: aa-sync is CPU-throttled from about 09:55 (flat 85% ceiling), likely from a reduced or mis-set CPU quota or limit, so its latency rises from about 90 ms to about 550 ms. portfolio-consumer's synchronous calls to it then slow and time out, queue consumption drops from about 49 to about 15 while publishing stays near 40, and portfolio-updates backs up from about 10:02, delaying notifications.
hypotheses.label: medium

supporting.text: aa-sync CPU throttle was at baseline (about 3%) until 09:54, first rose at 09:55, and reached a flat 85% by 09:59, where it stayed through the end of the window. aa-sync logs still reported 85% throttling at the end of the window.
aa-sync latency rose from a baseline of about 86-92 ms at the same time (first rise at 09:55) and stayed at about 520-580 ms.

portfolio-consumer calls aa-sync synchronously (weight 0.8), so an aa-sync slowdown propagates to it. Its latency rose from about 150 ms to about 285 ms at 09:55 and to about 510 ms by 10:00, and its aa-sync timeouts begin around 09:57.

The portfolio-updates queue's consume_rate dropped from about 49 to about 30 at the 09:55 point, while publish_rate stayed near 40. aa-sync publishes to this queue and portfolio-consumer consumes from it. The backlog warning first appeared at 10:02:53.
aa-sync request rate did not rise before or during the throttle onset (it fell slightly), which points to a quota or limit problem, or per-request cost, rather than extra load. This is an inference.

contradicting.text: portfolio-consumer rps stayed flat at about 40 after 10:00, which disagrees with a drop in queue consume_rate. Either the metrics measure different things or the mechanism is not fully understood.

The rate summaries (publish about 40 vs consume about 15) imply far faster backlog growth than the observed roughly 25 messages per minute. Units or metrics may be inconsistent, and this is an unverified assumption.
The flat 85.0 for about an hour may be a cap or a stuck reading rather than a true measurement. No configured CPU quota or change was found, and the change feed may be incomplete.
No restart, config or flag line appeared in aa-sync logs before onset, so the trigger is not identified.

hypotheses.statement: A separate fault on the msg-delivery or WhatsApp provider side, such as slow delivery receipts, delayed some notifications from about 09:02. This began 52 minutes before any aa-sync symptom and is independent of the portfolio-updates backlog. It could account for part of the late notifications that H1 and H3 do not explain.
hypotheses.label: low

supporting.text: msg-delivery logged delivery-receipt-delayed warnings starting at 09:02:32 and continuing to 10:58:09 (18 in total, complete). This is well before any aa-sync symptom.

contradicting.text: msg-delivery latency and rps were flat, the outbound-msgs queue stayed empty with 4 consumers, and there were no restarts and a low error rate. This shows no sign of a processing problem on the delivery side.

The 18 warnings carry only message IDs, with no type, template or 429 text. They cannot be linked to portfolio-update notifications, and rate limiting is not evident (based on absence of lines, not a targeted search).

hypotheses.statement: aa-sync's per-request CPU cost rose at about 09:55 because of an in-process CPU consumer that does not scale with request count, such as a background job, a heavier payload or consent mix, or a runaway loop. Throttling and latency climbed with no rise in rps, and the same downstream chain follows: consumer timeouts, a drop in queue consume_rate, and a growing portfolio-updates backlog.
hypotheses.label: low

supporting.text: Throttling rose from 3% to 85% while aa-sync rps stayed flat or fell, so a CPU consumer that does not scale with request count is plausible. The same downstream chain would follow.

Either the rate units or the queue consume metric is off, and the critic should check this.

actions.text: Check aa-sync's configured CPU limit/quota and recent changes (including infrastructure or orchestrator-level changes the change feed may not record). Raise the CPU limit or restore the previous value, and watch cpu_throttle_pct and latency return toward about 3% and about 90 ms.
actions.rationale: Throttling at a flat 85% with latency about 6x baseline and no rise in request rate is the leading cause of the slowdown, and removing the constraint should stop the queue backlog growing.

actions.text: After aa-sync recovers, monitor portfolio-updates consume_rate and depth until the backlog of about 1573 messages drains. If it does not drain, consider temporarily adding portfolio-consumer capacity.
actions.rationale: The queue was backed up with a steady 3 consumers while consume_rate sat well below publish_rate, so confirmation of recovery and drain is needed to know delayed notifications will be delivered.

actions.text: Confirm that queued portfolio-updates messages were delayed rather than lost, by searching portfolio-consumer logs for ack, retry, requeue and drop behaviour after aa-sync timeouts and checking the users reporting missing notifications.
actions.rationale: Some users reported notifications not arriving at all, but the dead-letter count was 0 and the fate of messages after a timeout was never searched.

actions.text: Add alerts on aa-sync cpu_throttle_pct and latency, and on portfolio-updates depth and consume_rate versus publish_rate. Reconcile the queue metric units and the mismatched summary-versus-point values.
actions.rationale: Throttling began at 09:55 and the backlog warning came only at 10:02, and the rate and unit inconsistencies limited this analysis.

actions.text: Once recovered, determine why aa-sync was throttled: compare the CPU request/limit history, per-request CPU cost and any background jobs, and review whether the flat 85.0 value reflects a real quota.
